elements.id-string-13: At the core of the Lax-Wendroff (LW) scheme lays the so-called LW procedure which relies on Taylor expanding  the solution in time up to second-order of accuracy, then replacing the time derivative by the space derivative according to the governing equations, and, finally, approximating the space derivatives by finite differences.

elements.id-string-16: When dealing with discontinuous solutions which may occur for any hyperbolic system of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs), the key point of most of numerical methods is their ability to dissipate appropriately.
elements.id-string-17: In other words extra dissipation must be added.
elements.id-string-18: The questions of where, when, and how much dissipation is to be added are of paramount importance to assure that the numerical method can handle smooth flows and discontinuous solutions equally well.
elements.id-string-19: Limiting second-order schemes has been achieved with slope or flux limiters relying on maximum principle preservation, or alternative related procedures.
elements.id-string-20: Beyond second-order accuracy, the limiting is not anymore a well-agreed subject of research.
elements.id-string-21: The most known technique is presumably the ENO/WENO procedure \cite{Shu1} for finite volume (FV) or finite differences (FD) schemes.
elements.id-string-22: Most of the limiting techniques rely on blending the first-order scheme/flux/reconstruction with a high-order one, using some \textit{a priori} sensor to determine where this blending would be appropriate.

elements.id-string-27: Contrarily, in this work we operate a shift and will couple the high-order CAT schemes with the \textit{a posteriori} MOOD limiting procedure \cite{CDL1,CDL2,CDL3}.
elements.id-string-28: The philosophical statement in MOOD is that it is easier to observe the inappropriate consequences of using a high-order scheme rather than predicting them with \textit{a priori} sensors.
elements.id-string-29: Consequently within a MOOD loop the unlimited high-order explicit scheme is used for the current time-step to produce a candidate numerical solution which is further tested against detection criteria stating if some cells are invalid.

elements.id-string-31: The goal of this paper is to provide a proof of concept for the design and validation of a CAT-MOOD scheme for systems of conservation laws.
